niche.title: WHAT DID TWO WORLD WARS CHANGE IN MEDICINE? #shorts #history
niche.description:
Penicillin was discovered in 1928, but the first patient treated with it died in 1941 because the supply ran out. This Short follows five medical advances that came out of the two world wars.

Blood transfusion moved from direct to indirect, blood banks appeared, and plastic surgery grew out of facial wounds. Wartime research pushed chemotherapy forward and made penicillin mass production possible by 1944. The 1918 flu also pushed countries to build health ministries and better systems for tracking disease.

niche.title: The Oldest Brain Surgery Was Better Than Civil War Medicine
niche.description:
Bone grows back around a hole in the skull only if the person lived for months. That one detail rewrites everything we assume about ancient surgery.

Studies of Neolithic and Bronze Age skulls put survival around 72% and higher — while early medieval survival sat near 50%. Nearly 800 Peruvian skulls show Inca-era survival above 75%.

Would you trust the flint, or the scalpel that came after it?

niche.title: MARIE CURIE and Her Science in WW1
niche.description:

niche.description:
How do you put a surgeon’s experience on a printed page?

First published in 1517, Hans von Gersdorff’s Feldtbuch der Wundarznei brought practical surgical knowledge into an illustrated book written in German for surgeons working in the field. Its woodcuts helped practitioners study wounds, instruments, and procedures in an era before modern anesthesia and antisepsis.

niche.title: How Did Gedroits Treat Belly Wounds in 1904? #Shorts
niche.description: In 1904, wounded soldiers near Mukden faced a terrible choice: a risky operation or almost certain death. Vera Gedroits, one of Russia’s first female surgeons, refused to accept the old rules about belly wounds. Working during the Russo-Japanese War, Gedroits studied injuries close to the fighting and pushed surgeons to operate sooner. Her work showed what happened when doctors stopped waiting for distant hospitals. niche.description:
Behind the roaring clash of forty thousand Roman legionaries, another battle was raging. A battle with no glory, no armor, and no modern medicine.

In this video, we step behind the lines of ancient Rome’s military machine into the valetudinarium—the field hospital. From the frontline combat medics (Capsarii) dragging mangled soldiers from the crush of battle, to the Greek surgeons performing brutal battlefield amputations with bronze saws and glowing-red cautery irons, discover the dark, gruesome, and surprisingly advanced reality of Roman military medicine.

niche.title: 10 Horrifying Ways Knights Really Died in Battle (Not Like the Movies)
niche.description:
You are on your knees in the mud at Agincourt, and the weight on your back will not let you rise. Your armour has worked. No sword has opened you. No arrow has found its gap. And you are going to die anyway — face-down, with no wound at all.

That is the knight Hollywood almost never shows you. The movies give him polished steel, a clear patch of ground and one worthy opponent. The real battlefield gave him mud, heat, a thousand men pushing from behind, a wound that turned days later — and an enemy that could kill an entire army without swinging a weapon once.

I'm Aliénor. These are ten real

niche.title: How Did Surgeons Operate Before Anesthesia?
niche.description:
How Did Surgeons Operate Before Anesthesia?

A leather strap between your teeth, strong men holding you down, a box of sawdust under the table, and a surgeon racing the clock. For thousands of years, this was surgery. In this video we follow how surgeons operated without anesthesia, from opium sponges and boiling oil to Frances Burney's harrowing letter, the laughing gas shows, the Ether Dome in Boston and the myth of Robert Liston's "300 percent" operation. Plus why it took almost half a century for anyone to take the answer seriously.

niche.description:
Before Dominique Jean Larrey, ambulances waited until the battle was over. In 1793, Napoleon's surgeon sent light horse-drawn wagons racing into the gunfire — and invented triage, battlefield surgery, and the modern ambulance itself.

niche.description: Imagine a soldier on a battlefield, wounded and in agony, with no medicine and no anaesthetic — and the surgeon hands him a bullet. He bites down on it, hard, because the operation is about to begin. Before modern anaesthesia, battlefield surgery was brutal: a surgeon had to cut, or even amputate, while the patient was wide awake, so soldiers were given something hard to bite on — a leather strap, a stick, or a lead bullet. niche.description: Some battlefield wounds were too swollen and dirty to close safely. In Iraq, a quiet medical tool gave surgeons something precious: time. Vacuum-assisted wound therapy used a sealed dressing and gentle suction to remove fluid and protect damaged tissue. The method came from the work of Louis Argenta and Michael Morykwas before military hospitals applied it to severe blast wounds. The story follows the treatment from its early design to Walter Reed and Landstuhl, where it helped surgeons manage wounds before final repair. niche.title: Les Petites Curies: Marie Curie's X-Ray Vans (1914)
niche.description:
September 1914. German troops are closing in on Paris, and Madame Marie Curie boards a government train to Bordeaux with one gram of radium – France's entire research supply – to keep it safe from the war.

Back in Paris she sees the real problem: surgeons at the front can't find the bullets and shrapnel inside the wounded. So she talks wealthy friends out of their cars, has them turned into mobile X-ray vans, learns to drive and takes her 17-year-old daughter Irène along as her assistant. The soldiers have a nickname for the vans: "les petites Curies" – the little Curies.

A wooden tablet from Vindolanda says one in ten men in a Roman auxiliary unit couldn’t work on a given day, and only six of them were wounded. This video follows what came next for a hurt soldier: first aid on the battlefield, surgery, the fortress hospital, the decision to send him back or discharge him, what it cost him in pay and legal standing, and what he did once he was out. niche.title: What If You Needed Surgery at Waterloo With No Anaesthetic?
niche.description:
In 1815, a wounded Redcoat lay wide awake on a door laid across 2 barrels while an Army surgeon amputated his shattered leg in a matter of minutes.

Forget the image of the cruel, clumsy battlefield butcher. At the Battle of Waterloo, experienced surgeons knew that speed was the real medicine. A leg smashed by a soft lead musket ball, taken off quickly on the same day, gave a man his best chance. Yet a single battalion of several hundred men might have just one surgeon, and around 50,000 were killed or wounded in one day.

niche.title: Brutal Surgery That Kept Rome Alive
niche.description:
Rome didn't build an empire solely with iron and discipline—its greatest weapon was what happened after the shields came down.

When young legionary Marcus is struck by a barbed arrow during an enemy horse archer ambush, survival comes down to the Roman army's frontline combat medics: the Capsari and field surgeons like Lucius. From field tourniquets to extraction spoons, honey dressings, and red-hot iron cauterization, discover the brutal realities of ancient military medicine that kept legions standing.

niche.description:
America built more than 200 fleet submarines in World War II — the Gato, Balao and Tench classes — and they sank over 1,300 enemy ships. Today, only 15 are left. And one of them is already sitting in the mud.

USS Silversides sank 23 ships on 14 war patrols — more than any other American submarine still in existence. In July 2026 she left her pier in Muskegon for the first time in nearly 40 years, towed across Lake Michigan for a $3.5 million dry docking. Her engines still run. Her propellers were removed decades ago.

A Gato-class submarine was drawn for a crew of sixty. On her war patrols, about eighty men lived aboard her, as one quartermaster of USS Gato remembered it. Where did they sleep, wash and breathe in a boat that small?
